cases.case_name: Thomas v. Sumner
cases.holding: The Court held that Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-205(a) obliges any person with reasonable cause to suspect abuse to report immediately, and that a reporter who meets that threshold acts in good faith and is immune under § 14-3-209, as are those who later participate in the investigation.
cases.quote: the plain language of § 14-3-205(a) does not require that the reporting party know that a child has been abused, or even reasonably believe that the child was abused

relevance.INP-01: Wyoming's reporting duty falls on 'any person,' so every mandated-reporter category at this node is governed by the § 14-3-205(a) reasonable-suspicion threshold this case construes.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms a voluntary third-party reporter is held to the same reasonable-suspicion threshold and enjoys the same § 14-3-209 immunity as a professional.
relevance.INP-05: A parent or caregiver who volunteers information during a child-protection inquiry participates in an act permitted by the Act and is covered by the statutory good-faith presumption.
relevance.INP-06: Anonymous or hotline reporters are shielded by the presumption of good faith, which negligence alone cannot overcome.
relevance.INP-07: The reporter here was a licensed social worker treating the child; the case sets the standard for clinical disclosures made without further investigation.
relevance.INP-08: Sets the threshold a school or other professional reporter must meet, and confirms no independent investigation is required before reporting.
relevance.INP-10: Because the report is lawful on mere reasonable suspicion, escalation from intake to investigation cannot be attacked by suing the reporter.
relevance.DEC-01: Even where a report is later screened out or unfounded, the reporter retains immunity unless bad faith is shown.
relevance.DEC-02: Immunity extends to participants in the ensuing investigation, which frames who may be sued once a report is accepted for assessment.

cases.case_name: Elmore v. Van Horn
cases.holding: The Court held Wyoming's child-abuse reporting statute confers qualified, not absolute, immunity: a reporter who reports in good faith is immune, good faith is presumed, and mere negligence in reporting does not defeat the presumption.
cases.quote: the Wyoming legislature intended to provide qualified immunity, that is immunity for all who report child abuse in good faith

relevance.*: This is the leading Wyoming statement of the reporter-immunity rule that governs who may be held liable for a child-abuse report at this decision point, and of the presumption of good faith a plaintiff must overcome.

cases.case_name: May v. Southeast Wyoming Mental Health Center
cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for the reporting therapist and the investigating public employees, holding that § 14-3-209 immunity is not confined to the act of reporting but covers participation in the investigation, and that the Governmental Claims Act separately immunized the state actors.
cases.quote: Section 14-3-209 does not limit immunity to suits based only on the reporting

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that the statutory immunity reaches everything a mandated reporter does under the Act, not just the initial call.
relevance.INP-02: Extends the same protection to non-professional participants who supply information after a report is made.
relevance.INP-06: Supports the confidentiality-and-immunity architecture behind Wyoming's hotline intake.
relevance.INP-07: The reporter was a mental-health professional; the case governs liability exposure for clinical disclosures.
relevance.DEC-01: Where a report is screened out or unfounded, neither the reporter nor the investigators lose immunity on that account alone.
relevance.OUT-06: Read with the Governmental Claims Act holding, it marks the narrow path to tort liability against state child-welfare actors.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of RTB
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the neglect adjudication, holding the State must prove neglect by a preponderance of the evidence, and cautioned that an officer taking warrantless protective custody under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-405(a)(i) must actually find the child seriously endangered rather than apply a blanket positive-drug-test policy.
cases.quote: During the adjudicatory hearing, the State had the burden to prove its allegations of neglect by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-03: The removal here was made by a Rawlins police officer, and the opinion states the reasonable-grounds test governing law-enforcement protective custody and referral.
relevance.INP-10: Illustrates how a medical report escalates to investigation, protective custody and petition, and the evidence each step requires.
relevance.INP-12: Directly construes § 14-3-405(a)(i): a blanket policy of taking custody on any positive parental drug test does not substitute for the statutory serious-endangerment finding.
relevance.DEC-03: Supplies the governing burden of proof for a founded finding of neglect at adjudication.
relevance.DEC-04: Requires a nexus between the reported risk factor and actual endangerment before emergency removal, and reviews the 48-hour shelter-care determination.
relevance.DEC-05: Describes the combined shelter-care and initial hearing that follows the filing of a neglect petition under § 14-3-409(c).
relevance.ACT-03: Explains the § 14-3-409(d) contrary-to-welfare finding required before legal custody is transferred for foster placement.
relevance.ACT-05: Shows the court's power to order continued shelter care as the protective measure short of adjudication.
relevance.ACT-06: The case arose from a medical-setting drug screen and the resulting safety assessment of the caregivers available to the child.
relevance.OUT-05: The preponderance standard stated here is what an unproven petition fails to meet, producing dismissal.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of AE
cases.holding: The Court affirmed an adjudication of neglect of an infant who failed to thrive at home but gained weight in hospital, holding that differences in a child's condition between care settings are competent evidence of neglect and that the appellate court will not reweigh the juvenile court's assessment.
cases.quote: we have recognized that differences in a child's condition between care settings can be evidence of neglect

relevance.INP-07: The referral came from the treating physician who took protective custody at the hospital, the paradigm medical disclosure.
relevance.INP-10: Shows the evidentiary picture that moves a medical report into a formal neglect investigation and petition.
relevance.DEC-03: Defines what evidence will sustain a founded finding of neglect under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-202(a)(vii).
relevance.ACT-06: The child's emergency hospitalization and medical monitoring were the protective interventions the court approved.
relevance.OUT-05: Because the parents complied, the child was returned and the case closed shortly after disposition, illustrating a non-removal outcome.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of NP
cases.holding: The Court held that the statutory right to a jury trial at a juvenile adjudicatory hearing is waived unless a written demand is filed within ten days of the advisement, and affirmed the neglect adjudication as supported by sufficient evidence.
cases.quote: we conclude that Mother waived her right to a jury trial when she failed to file a demand within the ten-day time frame required by statute

relevance.INP-04: Confirms that juvenile-court procedure, including advisements at the initial hearing, controls once a court opens a child-protection case.
relevance.DEC-03: Restates that neglect must be proven by a preponderance and sets the deference owed the juvenile court's finding.
relevance.DEC-05: Fixes the procedural consequences of the initial hearing on a neglect petition, including the ten-day jury demand.
relevance.OUT-04: The child was seventeen at adjudication, showing the juvenile court's authority over an older youth approaching majority.
relevance.OUT-05: A parent who loses the adjudication cannot obtain dismissal by reweighing evidence on appeal.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of AA
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding the juvenile court violated the father's due-process right to notice and an opportunity to be heard in the early stages of the case, and that 'other aggravating circumstances' relieving the Department of reasonable efforts under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-2-309(c)(v) must be as severe as the enumerated grounds.
cases.quote: the legislature logically meant for “other aggravating circumstances” to meet the same level of severity as set out in the preceding provisions

relevance.INP-04: Holds the State must give an identified, locatable parent notice of the proceedings from the outset.
relevance.DEC-04: A parent must be notified and heard on shelter care and placement even when removal was made on an emergency basis.
relevance.DEC-05: Sets the notice and hearing obligations that attach once the petition is filed and the case is opened.
relevance.ACT-02: Defines when a court may excuse court-ordered rehabilitative services altogether as an aggravated-circumstances case.
relevance.ACT-05: Shows the limits on protective orders and placements entered without hearing the absent parent.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts may not be waived on a thin record; the Department's duty to work toward return of the child was reinstated.
relevance.FAIL-01: A working example of appellate reversal of a juvenile-court order for procedural due-process error.

cases.case_name: FH v. State (In re Interest of ECH)
cases.holding: The Court held that Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-409(b) requires the juvenile court to advise parents of the right to counsel at the shelter-care hearing and to appoint counsel on request, that the right applies to a parent not accused of abuse or neglect, and that its denial before a permanency hearing ending reunification is plain error.
cases.quote: § 14-3-409(b) requires a juvenile court to advise the child's parents of their right to counsel at the shelter care hearing

relevance.INP-12: The advisement duty attaches at the shelter-care hearing that must follow emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: A parent whose child is removed is entitled to be advised of counsel at the first hearing after removal.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement ordered at shelter care cannot stand where the court failed to advise and appoint counsel.
relevance.OUT-01: Counsel is required where the hearing may end reunification efforts, the decision point that forecloses return home.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of SRS and LS
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the change of permanency plan from reunification to adoption, holding that parents are not entitled to an indefinite period to complete a case plan and that the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in finding adoption served the children's best interests after eighteen months of limited progress.
cases.quote: Parents are not afforded an indefinite period to achieve their case plan goals

relevance.INP-03: The case opened on police welfare checks that produced the neglect petition, the law-enforcement referral pathway.
relevance.ACT-02: Sets the time horizon within which court-ordered services must produce measurable progress.
relevance.ACT-03: Explains the conditions under which continued out-of-home foster placement is upheld at permanency review.
relevance.OUT-01: States the point at which a reunification plan may be abandoned notwithstanding some parental progress.
relevance.OUT-04: Shows how the fifteen-of-twenty-two-month clock drives permanency timing for children remaining in care.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of LH
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the change of permanency plan to adoption, holding that the possible separation of siblings is a factor the juvenile court must weigh at every stage of placement and permanency, but that the court here had and considered ample evidence of the sibling relationship.
cases.quote: the separation of siblings and the impact on the minor child in the Department's custody is a factor for the juvenile court to consider

relevance.ACT-04: The child was placed in relative foster care with a great-grandmother, and the opinion addresses how kin placement interacts with sibling ties.
relevance.OUT-04: Describes the six-month review and twelve-month permanency hearing structure governing a child's continued time in care.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of DT and NT
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a permanency-plan change to adoption, holding that whether the children should attend the permanency hearing should be decided before the hearing, but that deciding it afterward was not plain error and did not violate the mother's due-process rights.
cases.quote: A determination whether the children should be present at a permanency plan hearing should be made prior to the hearing

relevance.ACT-03: Addresses the procedural regularity required at the hearing that continues a child in foster placement.

cases.case_name: Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to ALRW
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-2-309(a)(iii), holding that the sufficiency of the Department's reasonable efforts is assessed case by case and that the Department must tie its efforts to the reasons that necessitated the child's out-of-home placement.
cases.quote: We assess whether sufficient evidence supports that DFS made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the family on a case-by-case basis

relevance.INP-03: The case began with a police welfare check and arrest that produced protective custody and a neglect petition.
relevance.DEC-06: Explains why services must be matched to the specific removal reasons, the premise of any alternative-response service plan.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary engagement in services is measured against the conditions that caused the removal.
relevance.ACT-02: Supplies the governing standard for whether court-ordered services amounted to reasonable efforts.
relevance.ACT-05: Illustrates the protective steps, including suspended visitation, ordered short of termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the reasonable-efforts showing the State must make before reunification may be abandoned.
relevance.PMC-01: Case-by-case judicial review of reasonable efforts is the state-court analogue of federal CFSR scrutiny.

cases.case_name: Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to PML and EGL
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding that whether the Department made reasonable efforts is assessed case by case, that its efforts must be accessible and tailored to the parent, and that a case plan adapted to a mother's intellectual disability satisfied the standard.
cases.quote: We assess on a case-by-case basis whether sufficient evidence exists to demonstrate the Department made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the family

relevance.ACT-02: States the controlling reasonable-efforts test for court-ordered service plans and how tailoring is judged.
relevance.OUT-01: Marks the point at which reasonable but unsuccessful efforts justify ending reunification.
relevance.OUT-02: Reasonable, unsuccessful efforts are an element the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence under § 14-2-309(a)(iii).
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court addressed the parent's argument that the Americans with Disabilities Act required further accommodation of her intellectual disability in the case plan.
relevance.PMC-01: Judicial case-by-case review of agency effort is the state check corresponding to federal permanency monitoring.

cases.case_name: ARC v. State, Department of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding the Department proved by clear and convincing evidence that it made reasonable rehabilitative efforts, and that under strict scrutiny the State must use the least intrusive means, though the Court did not decide whether guardianship is a less intrusive alternative to termination.
cases.quote: the district court properly concluded that DFS presented clear and convincing evidence it made reasonable efforts to reunite her with the children

relevance.ACT-02: Shows what a compliant family service plan looks like and when a parent's non-completion, not agency inaction, is the cause of failure.
relevance.OUT-01: Fixes the evidentiary showing required before reunification efforts may be declared unsuccessful.

cases.case_name: LS v. Johnson County Department of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a jury verdict terminating parental rights, holding that termination statutes are strictly scrutinized and must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and that neglect is assessed cumulatively rather than incident by incident.
cases.quote: Considering the evidence in the record in its entirety, there is clear and convincing proof sufficient to support the jury's findings of abuse and neglect

relevance.DEC-03: Explains that a founded finding rests on the accumulation of incidents and conditions over time, not a single event.
relevance.OUT-02: States the clear-and-convincing burden and the cumulative-evidence rule governing termination on abuse or neglect grounds.
relevance.OUT-05: The converse of the rule: isolated incidents that do not accumulate will not support termination.

cases.case_name: Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to RVR, KAR and RLR
cases.holding: The Court held that Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-2-318(a) creates neither a mandatory right to counsel nor a statutory right to effective assistance of counsel in termination proceedings, and affirmed the refusal to set aside an entry of default against the father.
cases.quote: Wyoming Statute § 14-2-318(a) does not create a statutory right to counsel or a statutory right to effective assistance of counsel in termination of parental rights cases

relevance.FAIL-01: Forecloses ineffective-assistance-of-counsel as a statutory ground for appellate reversal of a Wyoming termination order and sets the good-cause standard for setting aside default.

cases.case_name: BSC v. Natrona County Department of Family Services
cases.holding: Applying Lassiter and the Mathews v. Eldridge factors case by case, the Court held the district court did not deny the incarcerated, indigent father due process when it refused to appoint counsel for him at the hearing terminating his parental rights.
cases.quote: we conclude that BSC's due process rights were not violated when the district court refused to appoint counsel to represent him at the termination proceeding

relevance.FAIL-01: Defines the narrow circumstances in which denial of appointed counsel at a Wyoming termination hearing is reversible due-process error.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Guardianship of LNP
cases.holding: In Wyoming's principal Indian Child Welfare Act decision, the Court affirmed a permanent guardianship of an Indian child, holding that a communication giving the court reason to know the child was Indian triggered ICWA § 1912(a) notice, that a qualified expert witness under § 1912(e) need not have expertise in tribal customs, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the serious-damage finding.
cases.quote: neither the ICWA, nor the relevant BIA Guidelines, require a “qualified expert witness” to possess expertise in tribal customs

relevance.INP-11: This is the Wyoming Supreme Court's controlling application of ICWA notice, qualified-expert and evidentiary requirements once a child is identified as an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-03: A foster-care placement of an Indian child requires the § 1912(e) clear-and-convincing serious-damage finding supported by qualified expert testimony.
relevance.OUT-03: Sets the Wyoming standard for a permanent guardianship of an Indian child, including the parental-unfitness finding and the guardianship's revocability.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of JW v. State
cases.holding: The Court reversed a permanency order placing children with non-relative foster parents and remanded with instructions to place them with their uncle and aunt, rejecting the argument that the federal and state kinship-placement preferences are merely precatory.
cases.quote: We are unable to accept these characterizations given the high stakes in play here

relevance.ACT-04: This is the leading Wyoming authority that relative and kinship placement is a genuine preference the agency must actively pursue, not a box to check.
relevance.OUT-03: Supports kinship permanency as the preferred outcome where suitable relatives have been identified.
relevance.FAIL-01: A rare appellate reversal of an agency-driven permanency placement for failure to honor the kinship preference.

cases.case_name: SLB v. JEO
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the denial of a mother's petition to terminate the father's parental rights, holding the termination statutes are strictly construed and are not an avenue for one divorced parent to strip the other of the fundamental right to associate with a child.
cases.quote: We emphasize, however, the right to associate with one's child is a fundamental right

relevance.OUT-05: An example of a termination petition properly denied and dismissed on strict construction of the statutory grounds.

cases.case_name: Ailport v. Ailport
cases.holding: Applying Troxel, the Court held Wyoming's grandparent visitation statute must be read to require grandparents to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the parents are unfit or that their visitation decisions are or will be harmful before any best-interests inquiry, and affirmed denial of the grandparents' petition.
cases.quote: Parents have a fundamental due process right to guide the upbringing of their children, including determining the level of contact with their grandparents

relevance.INP-05: Confirms that a fit parent's own decisions about a child's care and contacts are entitled to constitutional deference when third parties seek state intervention.
relevance.ACT-04: Kin who seek contact or placement over a fit parent's objection must first overcome the constitutional presumption in the parent's favor.
relevance.OUT-03: Sets the constitutional threshold third-party relatives must clear before a court may order contact or custody arrangements.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of RMS
cases.holding: The Court affirmed an adoption granted without the mother's consent, holding the district court did not abuse its discretion in finding clear and convincing evidence that she willfully failed to support her child under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-22-110(a).
cases.quote: The district court did not abuse its discretion by concluding there was clear and convincing evidence that Mother willfully failed to support her child

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the Wyoming standard for adoption without parental consent, the alternative route to severing parental rights outside Title 14.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of ATWS
cases.holding: The Court reversed the denial of an adoption petition, holding the adoption statutes, read in light of their purpose of providing for the welfare of children, do not bar the petitioner from adopting where the existing parent's rights would be unaffected, and remanded for a best-interests determination.
cases.quote: The adoption statutes, whose purpose of providing for the welfare of children is the surest guide to their meaning, do not prohibit KA from adopting the Child

relevance.OUT-02: Removes a legal barrier to adoption where the child's existing legal parent retains rights, expanding permanency options.
relevance.OUT-03: Supports a permanency arrangement that adds a legal parent without displacing the existing one.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of MAJB
cases.holding: The Court held the district court had subject-matter jurisdiction to approve a Hague Convention adoption and was statutorily authorized to enter a decree permitting a Wyoming birth certificate with an accurate date of birth, and reversed the dismissal.
cases.quote: The district court has subject matter jurisdiction to approve the Hague Convention adoption

relevance.INP-11: Shows how federal and international adoption law overlays Wyoming juvenile jurisdiction in cases with a foreign or federal dimension.
relevance.FAIL-01: An appellate reversal correcting a lower court's erroneous refusal to exercise jurisdiction over a child's permanency status.

cases.case_name: Cline v. State, Department of Family Services
cases.holding: In wrongful-death suits arising from the deaths of two teenagers placed by the State in a private 24-hour care facility, the Court affirmed summary judgment for the State, holding the facility was an independent contractor and neither it nor its employee was a 'public employee' whose torts the Governmental Claims Act would reach.
cases.quote: as a matter of law, NSI was an independent contractor, and neither NSI nor its employee Edward Gillison was a “public employee” under the Claims Act

relevance.OUT-06: Defines the State's tort exposure when a child dies while placed in a contracted residential facility.
relevance.FAIL-04: Certification and regulatory oversight of a placement provider do not, without operational control, make the State answerable for the provider's negligence.
relevance.PMC-02: Marks the limit of financial accountability for contracted child-welfare providers under Wyoming law, leaving audit and licensure as the practical remedies.

cases.case_name: Circuit Court of the Eighth Judicial District v. Lee Newspapers
cases.holding: The Court held that court proceedings and judicial documents in child sexual-assault cases must generally remain open, with redaction and initials used to satisfy the victim-confidentiality statute, and that closure requires an on-the-record finding of a compelling interest, narrowly tailored, after a hearing open to the public.
cases.quote: the circuit court must find that there is a compelling interest in closing the court proceedings and sealing the case file which is essential to preserve higher values

relevance.INP-09: Public access to the court record is the mechanism by which outside observers detect systemic failures in child cases.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes that wholesale sealing of a child-related case file without findings is unlawful, the core transparency failure at this node.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the ability of citizen reviewers and the press to observe how child cases are actually handled.
relevance.PMC-05: Supplies the Wyoming constitutional and procedural test for overcoming the presumption of openness in child-related judicial records.
relevance.PMC-06: Openness of the underlying case records is the precondition for any external analysis of decision quality.

cases.case_name: Yellowbear v. State
cases.holding: In a felony-murder prosecution arising from the death of a child, the Court held that the location of the offense had been removed from the diminished Wind River Indian Reservation and was no longer Indian country, so Wyoming courts had jurisdiction.
cases.quote: Therefore, the State of Wyoming had jurisdiction to pursue the criminal charge

relevance.INP-11: Wyoming's jurisdictional line between state authority and Indian country turns on the reservation-boundary analysis this case performs.
relevance.ACT-06: The case concerns the fatal consequences of failing to obtain medical care for an injured child within Wyoming's jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: JET v. State, Department of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the refusal to let a young mother withdraw her admission of neglect, holding the juvenile court gave the statutorily required advisements at the initial hearing and did not abuse its discretion despite her claim of mental illness and her own earlier requests for help.
cases.quote: The juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in denying the appellant's motion to withdraw her admission of neglect

relevance.INP-04: Sets out the advisements a juvenile court must give a respondent parent at the initial hearing.
relevance.INP-05: The mother had sought help voluntarily from public-health and counseling services before the petition was filed, and the Court declined to treat that as a reason to undo the adjudication.
relevance.ACT-01: Shows the limits of the argument that voluntary help-seeking should insulate a family from formal court action.
relevance.DEC-05: Governs admissions entered on a neglect petition and the standard for withdrawing them.
relevance.OUT-05: Defines when a parent may and may not unwind an adjudication and obtain dismissal.

cases.case_name: Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to JJD
cases.holding: Reviewing for plain error, the Court held the mother was not denied a meaningful opportunity to be heard when the district court proceeded with the termination hearing and allowed her to appear and testify by telephone while her counsel appeared in person.
cases.quote: The district court did not deny Mother a meaningful opportunity to be heard when it proceeded with the termination hearing and allowed her to appear by phone

relevance.FAIL-01: Defines when a procedural irregularity at a termination hearing is and is not reversible plain error on appeal.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may permanently sever the rights of parents in their natural child, the Due Process Clause requires proof of the State's allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor that Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-2-309's clear-and-convincing standard implements at the termination decision.

cases.case_name: Troxel v. Granville
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The plurality held Washington's breathtakingly broad grandparent visitation statute unconstitutional as applied, because it gave no special weight to a fit parent's decision, and reaffirmed the presumption that fit parents act in their children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: When a parent asks for help rather than being accused, the constitutional presumption that the parent is acting in the child's interests still governs state responses.
relevance.DEC-01: Absent evidence of unfitness, the State must presume a parent's decisions are in the child's best interests, which is the constitutional premise for screening a report out.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship arrangements imposed over a fit parent's objection must give special weight to the parent's own decision.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held there is no absolute due-process right to appointed counsel for an indigent parent in a termination proceeding; the trial court must decide case by case under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.DEC-05: Sets the federal standard governing whether counsel must be appointed when the State opens a case seeking to sever the parent-child relationship.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal rule Wyoming applied in BSC to reject an automatic right to appointed counsel at termination.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held Illinois could not presume an unwed father unfit and take his children in a dependency proceeding without a hearing on his individual fitness, because the interest of a parent in the children he has raised is protected by due process and equal protection.
cases.quote: The rights to conceive and to raise one’s children have been deemed “essential,”

relevance.INP-12: Emergency state custody may not rest on a categorical presumption about a class of parents.
relevance.DEC-04: A removal decision must be based on an individualized fitness determination, not a blanket rule.
relevance.FAIL-02: Removing children without any hearing on the parent's fitness is the paradigm constitutional violation this node describes.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a State's failure to protect a child from private violence, even after the agency received repeated reports and took no action, does not violate the Due Process Clause, because the Clause imposes no affirmative duty of protection absent a custodial relationship.
cases.quote: we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.DEC-01: Screening out or under-responding to a report, however tragic the outcome, is generally not a federal constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to meet child-welfare performance expectations is addressed through funding and administrative remedies, not a § 1983 due-process claim.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the constitutional baseline against which liability for a child's death after agency contact is measured, and marks the custody exception that Tenth Circuit foster-care cases build on.
relevance.OUT-06: Defines when the State can and cannot be held constitutionally responsible for serious harm to a child known to the agency.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review and legislative reform, rather than constitutional litigation, are the principal accountability routes after a child death.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the 'reasonable efforts' clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act does not unambiguously confer an enforceable federal right on the Act's beneficiaries and Congress created no private remedy, leaving enforcement to the Secretary's funding mechanisms and state judicial findings.
cases.quote: we think that Congress did not intend to create a private remedy for enforcement of the “reasonable efforts” clause

relevance.INP-09: Federal oversight of state performance runs through administrative review and funding conditions rather than private suit.
relevance.DEC-06: Front-end prevention obligations under Title IV-E are enforceable administratively, not by individual families in federal court.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the controlling authority on how a state's federal child-welfare compliance failures may and may not be remedied.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR review and program improvement plans, not litigation, are the federal monitoring lever.
relevance.PMC-02: Locates accountability for Title IV-E funds in the Secretary's audit and funding-reduction powers.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the role of administrative and citizen review bodies as the practical check on state plan compliance.
relevance.PMC-05: Because private enforcement is unavailable, public disclosure of compliance data is the principal transparency tool.
relevance.PMC-06: Frames what an external analysis layer can accomplish where no private right of action exists.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under the Indian Child Welfare Act is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation take the reservation domicile of their mother, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States

relevance.INP-11: Determines when a Wyoming state court must yield exclusive jurisdiction to a tribal court over an Indian child's custody proceeding.
relevance.FAIL-05: Enforces ICWA's protections against practices that would route Indian children out of tribal jurisdiction, a recognized form of systemic bias.

cases.case_name: Gomes v. Wood
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit adopted the majority rule that state officials may remove a child without prior notice and a hearing only on a reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the child's safety, found fact questions on whether that standard was met, but granted qualified immunity because the law was not clearly established.
cases.quote: officials may remove a child from the home without prior notice and a hearing when they have a reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the safety of the child

relevance.INP-12: This is the controlling circuit standard governing warrantless emergency protective custody of a child in Wyoming.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the constitutional test an agency's emergency removal decision must satisfy and the prompt post-deprivation hearing that must follow.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines the threshold below which a removal is an unconstitutional seizure actionable under § 1983 in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Woodard
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed qualified immunity for a caseworker who visually examined a four-year-old's unclothed body at her preschool without a warrant or parental consent, holding the plaintiffs failed to show clearly established law that the special-needs doctrine could not justify the search.
cases.quote: We conclude they have not shown clearly established law that the special needs doctrine could not support the search in this case

relevance.INP-08: Governs the constitutionality of a caseworker's examination or interview of a child conducted at school without parental notice.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets the Fourth Amendment framework and the qualified-immunity hurdle for investigative searches and interviews of a child.
relevance.FAIL-02: Shows how difficult it is to establish liability for an intrusive investigative search absent clearly established circuit law.

cases.case_name: Dahn v. Amedei
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit recognized that a foster child harmed by the State may sue under the special-relationship doctrine, but reversed the denial of qualified immunity because it was not clearly established that out-of-state caseworkers had a special relationship with a child placed across state lines.
cases.quote: When a state fails to protect a foster child from harm, the foster child can sue the state under the special-relationship doctrine

relevance.ACT-03: Defines the constitutional duty the State assumes toward a child once it takes custody and places the child in foster care.
relevance.OUT-06: States the doctrinal basis for liability when a child in state custody suffers serious harm, and its qualified-immunity limits.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the special-relationship elements a family must plead when a child is injured or dies under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: Illustrates the interstate placement gaps that fatality and serious-injury reviews are meant to surface.

cases.case_name: Roska v. Sneddon
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to caseworkers who removed a chronically ill child from his home without a warrant or pre-deprivation hearing, holding their failure to offer reasonably available preventive services that would have eliminated the need for removal was objectively unreasonable.
cases.quote: In light of these circumstances, Defendants' failure to provide the Roskas with preventive services to eliminate the need for removal was not reasonable

relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal is unreasonable where reasonably available preventive services would have eliminated the need to remove the child.
relevance.DEC-06: Directly supports an alternative-response duty: services capable of averting removal must be considered before the child is taken.
relevance.ACT-01: Establishes that voluntary and preventive services are not optional courtesies when they would obviate removal.
relevance.INP-12: Removal without a warrant or pre-deprivation hearing deprived the family of a clearly established right to family integrity.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the circuit's clearest example of an unlawful removal surviving qualified immunity.

cases.case_name: In re "H" Children
cases.holding: Over a two-justice dissent, the Court affirmed a juvenile-court adjudication of neglect and the ensuing placement order, holding that neglect need be shown only by a preponderance of the evidence and that the record contained sufficient evidence to sustain the finding under the statutory definition of a neglected child.
cases.quote: Child neglect, on the other hand, need only be shown by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.DEC-03: This is the source Wyoming authority for the preponderance standard that governs a founded finding of neglect at adjudication, and it sets out the deferential sufficiency review applied to that finding.
relevance.OUT-05: It states the converse of the rule: a petition the State cannot carry by a preponderance fails, and a parent who shows neither error nor prejudice cannot obtain dismissal on appeal.
relevance.DEC-05: The Court held the notice and opportunity to be heard due a parent after a neglect petition is filed are proportionate to the magnitude of the infringement, which is less than at a termination proceeding.
relevance.INP-03: The case began when Cheyenne police officers responding to a report of a possible suicidal subject encountered the children, and the county attorney filed the neglect petition two days later.

cases.case_name: KC v. State (In re GC)
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the change of the permanency plan from family reunification to adoption, holding that the State must prove the grounds for a change of permanency plan by a preponderance of the evidence and that the mother's repeated failures to appear for and to pass drug testing satisfied that burden.
cases.quote: when a change in the permanency plan is sought, the burden upon the State is to prove grounds for that change by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.ACT-02: This is the authority Wyoming's later opinions rest on when measuring a parent's progress under a court-ordered case plan, and it holds that parents have a due-process right to meaningful participation at the hearing where that progress is judged.
relevance.OUT-01: It fixes the burden and the procedural protections that apply at the precise point a reunification plan is abandoned for another permanency goal.

cases.case_name: RH v. State, Department of Family Services (In re DRS)
cases.holding: The Court affirmed orders placing the children with their grandparents and their father rather than returning them to the mother, holding that whether the Department made reasonable efforts is determined case by case and that the record supplied sufficient evidence of efforts to prevent removal and of the children's best interests.
cases.quote: Reasonable efforts are determined on a case-by-case basis.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the origin of Wyoming's case-by-case reasonable-efforts inquiry that the 2023 and 2024 termination opinions restate, and it catalogs the concrete services previously held sufficient.
relevance.DEC-06: The opinion applies Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-429(a)(iv), which it notes requires clear and convincing evidence that reasonable efforts were made to prevent the initial removal, the front-end prevention duty at this node.
relevance.OUT-01: A practitioner contesting whether the Department did enough before reunification was abandoned cites this case for the governing standard rather than only its later restatements.
relevance.ACT-04: The disposition upheld here placed two of the children with their grandparents, illustrating relative placement as the alternative to returning children to the parent.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights to TJH (Herden v. State ex rel. Department of Family Services)
cases.holding: Applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, the Court affirmed the termination, holding the defaulted mother's due-process rights were not violated when the district court held the evidentiary default hearing by video conference and limited her participation to cross-examination and argument rather than permitting her to present her own best-interests evidence.
cases.quote: Balancing the Mathews factors, it is clear Mother received adequate process under the circumstances of this case even though she was not permitted to present evidence on Child's best interests

relevance.FAIL-01: This is Wyoming's companion due-process authority to ECH and JJD on a parent's meaningful opportunity to be heard, and it fixes how far a court may limit a defaulted parent's participation before the order becomes reversible.
relevance.DEC-05: It shows the consequences of failing to answer a petition that opens a case to sever the parent-child relationship, including entry of default and the narrowed participation that follows.

cases.case_name: Northern Arapaho Tribe v. State (In re SNK)
cases.holding: Over a dissent, the Court held the Northern Arapaho Tribe's appeal from an order continuing an enrolled Indian child's placement in a non-Indian foster home was moot because the child had since been placed elsewhere, and it expressly declined to decide whether the 'existing Indian family' exception to the Indian Child Welfare Act applies in Wyoming.
cases.quote: we conclude that the issue in this case regarding the applicability of ICWA and the "existing Indian family" exception to ICWA is moot

relevance.INP-11: This is Wyoming's only other Indian Child Welfare Act appearance, and it establishes that whether the 'existing Indian family' exception applies in Wyoming is an important but expressly undecided question that counsel must brief from federal and out-of-state authority.

cases.case_name: Freudenthal v. Cheyenne Newspapers, Inc.
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the order compelling release of the budget-reduction plans the Department of Family Services and the Department of Health had submitted to the Governor, holding the plans were factual rather than deliberative, and declined to decide whether the Wyoming Public Records Act incorporates a deliberative process privilege at all.
cases.quote: The plans contain factual information, rather than opinions, deliberations or thought processes and are not, therefore, the sort of documents protected by the deliberative process privilege.

relevance.FAIL-06: This is the Wyoming decision that actually controls an executive agency's refusal to release child-welfare records: factual agency documents must be disclosed under the Public Records Act and a claimed deliberative privilege will not shield them.
relevance.PMC-05: It supplies the Wyoming Public Records Act framework and the narrow construction of exemptions under which a records request to the Department of Family Services must be litigated.
relevance.PMC-06: Access to the agency's own factual records is the precondition for any external cross-analysis of Wyoming child-welfare performance.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen and press review of agency policy depends on the disclosure obligation this case enforces against the executive branch.
relevance.PMC-02: The withheld records were the Department of Family Services' own budget-reduction plans, precisely the class of financial documents a funding audit depends on.
relevance.INP-09: Public disclosure of agency records is how outside oversight bodies obtain the material that triggers systemic review.

cases.case_name: In re WDW
cases.holding: Where a termination-of-parental-rights petition is filed by someone other than an authorized agency, Wyo. Stat. Ann. 14-2-314 requires the court to direct that a social study be made by the county public-assistance/social-services office, and that direction should issue when the petition is filed; on these facts, however, the father intentionally waived the timing objection by asking the court to try the case without the study, and he failed to show prejudice from the study's late completion or from its omission of a personal interview with him, so the termination order was affirmed.
cases.quote: The statutory language is mandatory and the social study should have been ordered when the petition was filed.

relevance.INP-04: This is the clearest Wyoming holding that a court order directing the child-welfare agency to investigate and assess a family is a mandatory, statutorily triggered step in a civil child-welfare proceeding, which is exactly the INP-04 court-ordered-referral trigger.

notes: Wyoming has no intermediate appellate court; every state case here is a published Wyoming Supreme Court opinion (court_id 'wyo'). The federal circuit for Wyoming is the Tenth Circuit (ca10), used for the Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment and 42 U.S.C. section 1983 removal and foster-care nodes.

Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener on 2026-09-20 and its opinion text read; each quote was verified programmatically to be an exact substring of the retrieved majority-opinion text after normalizing whitespace and curly quotation marks. No unpublished memorandum decisions were used.

Citation form: Wyoming adopted a public-domain citation (e.g. '2024 WY 75') in 2001, and it is given first with the Pacific Reporter parallel cite. Two published opinions - Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to RVR, KAR and RLR, 2022 WY 153, and Ailport v. Ailport, 2022 WY 43 - carry no P.3d parallel citation in the CourtListener cluster record, so only the public-domain cite is given; a practitioner should add the P.3d cite from a commercial reporter (both are marked 'Published' by CourtListener).

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the WY node files are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations. Of those candidate titles, seven were retrieved and kept because they are genuinely on point: In re Guardianship of LNP (styled In the Matter of the Guardianship of LNP), In re Adoption of ATWS, In re Adoption of MAJB, In re L.H. v. State (In the Interest of LH), Alcorn v. State ex rel. Dep't of Family Services (Matter of TPR to ALRW), Roberts v. State, Dep't of Family Services, and the JJD termination case. Titles such as 'In the Matter of the Petition for Withdrawal of Bar Member: Collin C. Hopkins' and 'In the Matter of the Sanction Fee of Christopher Goetz' are attorney-discipline and criminal-fee matters with no child-welfare content and were discarded, as were the Webb and Noe child-support-enforcement cases.

ICWA: Wyoming has essentially one substantive Indian Child Welfare Act decision, In the Matter of the Guardianship of LNP, 2013 WY 20, 294 P.3d 904 (section 1912(a) notice trigger, section 1912(e) qualified expert witness who need not have tribal-customs expertise, and the serious-damage finding). Repeated CourtListener searches of the Wyoming Supreme Court found no published state decision on ICWA placement preferences under 25 U.S.C. section 1915, on transfer to tribal court under section 1911(b), or on 'active efforts' as an independent agency duty - LNP declined to reach active efforts because the appellant cited no authority and because the petitioners were private grandparents, not the State. Wyoming has no state ICWA statute. For those points the federal standard governs, and Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield is supplied for exclusive tribal jurisdiction; Yellowbear v. State supplies the Wyoming Indian-country boundary analysis that determines whether a case arises in Indian country at all.

No published Wyoming decision was found on extended foster care or continued juvenile-court jurisdiction past age 18 (OUT-04). The cases mapped there address the six-month review and twelve-month permanency structure of Wyo. Stat. Ann. section 14-3-431 and an adjudication of a seventeen-year-old, which is the closest published authority. Wyoming's Chafee/extended-care program is administered under Department of Family Services rule rather than litigated case law.

No published Wyoming decision was found squarely on (a) screening criteria or the decision to screen a report out (DEC-01), (b) a formal differential/alternative response track (DEC-06), (c) a central registry of substantiated findings and the due-process hearing rights attached to being listed on it, or (d) children who go missing from foster care. Wyoming's Child Protective Services Act, Wyo. Stat. Ann. sections 14-3-201 to 14-3-216, contains no central-registry due-process provision of the kind litigated in other states, which is why no registry case appears. For DEC-01 and DEC-06 the brief supplies the federal standard (DeShaney; Suter v. Artist M.; Troxel) plus Roska v. Sneddon's preventive-services duty, and says so here.

No Wyoming decision was found on a stand-alone civil protective or restraining order used to remove an alleged abuser instead of the child (ACT-05); the cases mapped there are the nearest analogues - shelter-care and emergency placement-review orders and suspended visitation under the Child Protection Act.

The FAIL-03, FAIL-06 and all six PMC oversight nodes have no Wyoming child-welfare case law. They are populated with the controlling federal authority on enforceability of Title IV-E obligations (Suter v. Artist M.: no private right to enforce 'reasonable efforts'), the constitutional floor (DeShaney), and the two Wyoming transparency decisions that actually control access to state agency records and child-related court files (Freudenthal v. Cheyenne Newspapers; Circuit Court of the Eighth Judicial District v. Lee Newspapers).

Practice points a lawyer should know. (1) Wyoming's reporting duty in Wyo. Stat. Ann. section 14-3-205(a) runs to 'any person' - there is no separate mandated-reporter class - and section 14-3-209 immunity is qualified, presumed, and extends beyond the report to participation in the investigation (Thomas v. Sumner; Elmore v. Van Horn; May). (2) The adjudication burden is a preponderance under section 14-3-425(a), while termination requires clear and convincing evidence under section 14-2-309(a) - do not conflate them. (3) A jury may be demanded at the adjudicatory hearing but only in writing within ten days of the advisement (In the Interest of NP). (4) There is a statutory advisement-and-appointment-of-counsel right at the shelter-care hearing under section 14-3-409(b) (FH v. State), but the Court has held section 14-2-318(a) creates neither a mandatory right to counsel nor a right to effective assistance in termination cases (Roberts), and Lassiter/BSC govern the constitutional claim - this is the single most consequential gap for parents in Wyoming.

In the Interest of RTB, 2024 WY 75, is the most useful recent authority for challenging a removal: the Court expressly said it 'would be concerning' if a police department took protective custody based solely on a parent's positive drug test without the section 14-3-405(a)(i) serious-endangerment analysis, and accepted that a nexus must exist between the risk factor and the neglect alleged, while still affirming on the fuller record. The Court also noted in footnote 3 that its precedent does not clearly set the burden of proof at a shelter-care hearing - an open question.

Troxel v. Granville is a plurality opinion; the quoted presumption that fit parents act in their children's best interests comes from Justice O'Connor's lead opinion, which the Wyoming Supreme Court adopted as controlling in Ailport v. Ailport, 2022 WY 43. Lassiter's CourtListener date_filed is 1981-08-28 (the rehearing-related date in that cluster record); the case was argued and decided in the October 1980 Term.

In the Interest of JW v. State, 2010 WY 28, 226 P.3d 873, is the strongest Wyoming authority for families seeking kinship placement - the Court reversed and ordered placement with the uncle and aunt and refused to treat the federal and state kinship preferences as merely precatory. The full sentence stating that preference at paragraph 27 contains an OCR error in CourtListener's text ('cireumstances'), so a shorter, clean sentence from the same discussion is quoted instead; counsel should quote paragraph 27 from the Pacific Reporter.

Several older Wyoming opinions in CourtListener (pre-2015 Harvard/LEXIS scans) contain OCR artifacts and embedded star-pagination markers. Quotes were deliberately selected from passages free of those artifacts; where a leading sentence was unusable for that reason it is flagged above. For the same reason the Santosky quote is the second half of the sentence at 455 U.S. 747-48, whose first half is broken by a star-pagination marker in the retrieved text.

Added In re "H" Children, 2003 WY 155, 79 P.3d 997, for DEC-03, OUT-05, DEC-05 and INP-03: it is the source Wyoming authority RTB and DRS cite for the preponderance standard at a neglect adjudication, it states the proportionality principle governing the process due a parent under the Child Protection Act, and the referral came from police responding to a welfare call. Two cautions for users: the adjudication was made under the 2003 numbering, Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-402(a)(xii)(A), not § 14-3-202(a)(vii) as the verifier's note stated, and Justice Golden dissented joined by Chief Justice Hill - the quote is from Justice Voigt's majority opinion.

Added KC v. State (In re GC), 2015 WY 73, 351 P.3d 236, for ACT-02 and OUT-01: the unanimous Court held parents have a due process right to meaningful participation at a hearing changing permanency away from family reunification, and fixed the State's preponderance burden for obtaining that change. Caution for practitioners: the sentence SRS and LS attributes to this case ('Parents are not afforded an indefinite period to achieve their case plan goals') does not appear verbatim anywhere in the CourtListener text of GC retrieved on 2026-09-20, which is an OCR scan carrying numerous artifacts ('cireumstances', '§ 14-2-809' for '§ 14-2-309'); the quote given here was taken from a clean passage of the majority opinion, and counsel should verify any GC language against the Pacific Reporter.

Added RH v. State, Dep't of Family Servs. (In re DRS), 2011 WY 128, 261 P.3d 697, for ACT-02, DEC-06, OUT-01 and ACT-04: it is the origin of Wyoming's case-by-case reasonable-efforts inquiry restated in ALRW and PML, it applies Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-429(a)(iv)'s requirement of clear and convincing evidence that reasonable efforts were made to prevent the initial removal, and the disposition it affirmed placed two of the children with their grandparents.

Added Matter of Termination of Parental Rights to TJH, 2021 WY 56, 485 P.3d 408, for FAIL-01 and DEC-05: it is Wyoming's companion due-process authority to ECH and JJD, applying Mathews v. Eldridge to a defaulted parent and fixing how far a court may limit her participation at the termination hearing before the order becomes reversible. Chief Justice Davis, joined by Justice Fox, concurred specially to correct a misreading of In re ZMETS; the quote is from the majority.

Added Northern Arapaho Tribe v. State (In re SNK), 2003 WY 141, 78 P.3d 1032, for INP-11: the Tribe's challenge to the juvenile court's application of the 'existing Indian family' exception was dismissed as moot over Justice Golden's dissent, and the majority said in terms that the exception's applicability in Wyoming 'is an important issue that needs to be addressed' but declined to address it. INP-11 should therefore be read as disclosing an open question rather than implying the point has never arisen. CourtListener carries this case under two clusters - 2549394, styled In re SNK, and 5322273, styled Northern Arapaho Tribe v. State - and cluster 2549394 was the one retrieved and read.

Added Freudenthal v. Cheyenne Newspapers, Inc., 2010 WY 80, 233 P.3d 933, for FAIL-06, PMC-05, PMC-06, PMC-03, PMC-02 and INP-09: FAIL-06 was the only node in the reconciled brief carrying fewer than two authorities, and the earlier transparency note cited Freudenthal without the brief containing an entry for it. The case is squarely on point - the withheld records were the Department of Family Services' own budget-reduction plans - and it holds factual agency documents must be released under the Wyoming Public Records Act while expressly leaving open whether the Act incorporates a deliberative process privilege at all.
